title: Package and update the Electron desktop application
summary: The desktop application is a small Electron shell with a pinned pnpm. One release number fixes the exact harness version, the application owns a reserved desktop profile, and an update replaces the whole release.
firstReason: The goals (no runtime to install, one release identity, a reserved profile, one update flow) stand, but the shell is a Go webview application, and there is no bundled pnpm because plugins are not npm packages.

title: Bundle the Desktop runtime and retain external plugins
summary: The desktop build ships the production package graph as application resources so nothing is installed at first start, while npm plugins installed by the user live in the desktop profile and survive upgrades.
firstReason: A Go desktop binary already contains its runtime; the part to keep is that user-installed plugins and their state live outside the application bundle and survive upgrades, as plugin processes.

title: Desktop welcome window material
summary: The desktop welcome and sign-in window is a separate native Electron window with its own small React bundle and a narrow preload bridge; it reuses the web launch URL for authentication and adds no host endpoint.
firstReason: First-run onboarding with one clear startup owner is kept, but it is a page served by the Go host inside the webview shell; whether the blurred native window material is available depends on the shell library.

title: Run Desktop through the shared Web application
summary: The desktop application runs the same web application through the same profile runner; the native shell owns only windows, menus, native dialogs, recovery and updates, and there is no second backend.
firstReason: This is the decision DH-ADR-3 already takes for the Go design: one UI, wrapped by a native shell.

title: Native Desktop fatal recovery
summary: A fatal start-up failure in the desktop application shows one native dialog per process, independent of the web page, with a bounded diagnostic, a crash-report file, and the choices exit, restart, or disable third-party bundles and restart.
firstReason: A recovery path that does not depend on the failing page is needed for any webview shell; disabling third-party bundles becomes disabling plugin processes.

title: Desktop close shortcuts follow page focus
summary: The close shortcut closes the focused sidebar page; only when no page can close does it close the desktop window. A stale target never falls back to another page or to the window.
firstReason: This is user-visible desktop behaviour, and on Windows closing the last window stops the host, so the no-fallback rule protects running work. The Go desktop shell (DH-ADR-3) implements it with its own menu and window calls.

title: Account-scoped Platform browser storage
summary: The embedded Platform page gets browser storage partitioned by a hash of the origin and the account id, so dismissed notices persist per account. Opening a partition clears everything except localStorage, and a disposable partition is used while the account id is unknown.
firstReason: The goal stands: page preferences persist per account and no credentials are left behind. Electron session partitions are the mechanism; a system webview hosted by a Go shell has different, per-platform storage controls, so the desktop spec must restate this with what the chosen shell supports.

title: Hide the Desktop window on close and confirm interruptible quits
summary: Closing the desktop window hides it and leaves the host running; Windows gets a tray icon and a first-close notice. Quitting asks the host whether agents, jobs or scheduled reminders would stop, and shows a confirmation only when they would.
firstReason: It prevents losing the current page state on close and cutting running tasks on quit without warning. The behaviour is independent of Electron; the Go shell (DH-ADR-3) needs a tray icon, a native message box and a host query for active work.

title: Desktop shell configuration independent of the Host
summary: The desktop shell owns its own settings file for anything it needs before the host starts or while the host is down (updates, crash recovery). Host and plugin settings stay in loader configuration.
firstReason: Ownership follows runtime dependency: a function that must work without the host cannot read host configuration. The rule holds for a Go shell process; if shell and host become one process the split may collapse, which the desktop spec must decide.

title: Desktop primary runtime
summary: The desktop application ships Python, Node.js, pnpm and data-processing and Office libraries as one release-bound payload that a path-query tool installs into the harness home and reports by absolute path. It never changes `PATH` or package-manager configuration, and installation publishes a complete staged copy.
firstReason: Agents on machines without development tools still need predictable interpreters. This is a payload for the agent's work, not a dependency of the host, so it applies to a Go desktop shell too; publishing a completed staged copy is the right failure behaviour.

title: Retained Desktop browser webviews
summary: On desktop the sidebar browser uses an Electron `<webview>` guest instead of an iframe, so it can show sites that refuse embedding and observe navigation. Pages stay alive across tab and layout changes, and storage partitions are keyed by workspace so related pages share sign-ins.
firstReason: The desktop shell becomes a system webview hosted by Go, which has no Electron guest tag. The goal (a retained, navigable browser pane with per-workspace storage) needs a new mechanism or a recorded limit; this is an open question for the desktop area.

title: Web install icons and launch display
summary: The Web app's install manifest carries four icons rendered from the official application tile (192 and 512 pixel, a maskable 512 pixel and a 180 pixel Apple touch icon) and requests `standalone` display in place of `fullscreen`. A browser test measures the maskable icon's safe area.
firstReason: Install icons and the manifest are static files that the Go host serves unchanged. The icon rendering script is upstream build tooling and is not carried over as such.

title: Desktop mandatory-update API
summary: Proposal, backend integration in progress upstream: a guest-accessible endpoint, `GET /api/v0/check_client_update`, tells the desktop application whether its version must be updated before use, with explicit success, blocking and error semantics, kept separate from the choice of update artifacts.
firstReason: Adopt if the Go desktop application keeps the same business server: the endpoint is an external service contract and does not depend on the shell technology. The desktop area must confirm the service exists before making it a deliverable.

title: Deferred Desktop update extensions
summary: Proposal, explicitly deferred upstream: possible later desktop update features (independently revised desktop packages with a `.dsk.N` version suffix, a stable channel, installation on next launch, replacing a pending update), none of them a requirement of the first update flow.
firstReason: Keep the decision as upstream made it, which is to defer: none of the candidates is built or approved, and each adds installer states. They are recorded so that the Go update design does not rule them out, for example by keeping full SemVer comparison.

title: Desktop update policy and installation
summary: Proposal recording the outstanding release and backend work for desktop updates: automatic discovery, user-initiated download, visible preparation state and a separate restart approval that accounts for running tasks, with signed Windows and macOS upgrades qualified end to end.
firstReason: Adopt the policy (discover automatically, download and restart only with approval, never interrupt running tasks silently). The installer mechanism upstream belongs to the Electron application; the Go desktop shell under DH-ADR-3 needs its own verified update mechanism.

title: Parallel macOS notarization from isolated App copies
summary: The macOS desktop release signs one application bundle, makes two isolated copies, and notarizes the update archive and the disk image in parallel, because stapling modifies the bundle and the two Apple submissions would otherwise run one after the other.
firstReason: A macOS desktop release still has to be signed and notarized, so the goal stands. The steps described are specific to electron-builder; the desktop shell is a Go webview application (DH-ADR-3) with its own packaging, and the desktop area decides whether two parallel submissions are still worth the complexity.

title: Windows runtime signature cache
summary: Windows packaging caches the signed copies of unchanged bundled runtime files (Python, LibreOffice), keyed by content, certificate and signing tool, so that a build does not repeat hardware-token signing and timestamping for files that did not change.
firstReason: Upstream build process: a speed optimisation of upstream's Windows packaging pipeline for the third-party runtimes it re-signs on every build. It carries no product behaviour; a Go packaging pipeline can add a cache later if it re-signs the same files.

title: Separate Windows hardware signing from timestamp completion
summary: Windows code signing is done in two separate phases: sign a private copy once with the hardware token and no timestamp, then add the timestamp without credentials, retrying only the timestamp at most three times. A hardware or verification failure keeps the interlock and is never recovered automatically.
firstReason: A Go Windows binary and installer are signed with the same tool, certificate and hardware token, so the failure analysis holds unchanged: a timestamp-server error must not cause a second use of the private key. The desktop and release area should keep the two-phase rule.

title: Remove the Desktop production profile core-package cleanup
summary: The desktop application no longer deletes or prunes packages in the profile's `node_modules` before starting the host; resolution order alone decides which copy of a package runs.
firstReason: npm tooling: the note is about `node_modules`, pnpm overrides and lock files inside a profile. A Go profile holds configuration only, because capabilities are compiled in or run as plugin processes.

title: Keyless browser e2e lane for the web GUI
summary: The web UI has a deterministic browser test lane that needs no API key: recorded sessions are replayed as model output against the real assembled host, a real browser drives the page, and the visible states are compared with normalized accessibility-tree snapshots.
firstReason: Replaying recorded model output into the real host while a real browser drives the real page is the right keyless evidence for a server-rendered UI too. The recordings must be made in the Go session format (DH-ADR-2) and the snapshots re-taken for the new HTML, so nothing is reused except the method.

title: Qualify Desktop update downloads with an isolated local server
summary: Desktop update downloads are qualified locally by running the real updater code against a loopback server that serves a test feed and inert bytes, with the installer call replaced by an observation, so no cloud storage or hardware signing is needed for a feedback cycle.
firstReason: The goal, exercising the real update path without release infrastructure, stands. The mechanism is built on Electron's updater classes; the Go desktop shell (DH-ADR-3) has a different updater and needs its own loopback qualification.

title: Preserve installed Desktop update evidence across restarts
summary: When a qualification run sets a journal directory, each desktop process writes a small log of whitelisted update states and actions to it, so that evidence survives the installer replacing the application. Raw errors, addresses and chat content are never written.
firstReason: An installed update ends the process that observed it in any desktop technology, so the evidence problem remains. The journal belongs to the Go desktop shell's updater (DH-ADR-3) and is redesigned with it; the whitelisting rule should be kept.

title: Isolate installed-update materials from releases and user data
summary: The two versions needed for an installed-update walkthrough are prepared under a random test identity and a separate distribution namespace, with their own user-data directory, so that test builds can never be offered to real clients or touch real user data.
firstReason: Isolation of test update material from real releases and user data is still required. The preparation steps operate on upstream's Electron runtime descriptor and inventory, which the Go desktop packaging (DH-ADR-3) does not have.

title: Web lane moves spreadsheet selections by keyboard before reflow assertions
summary: A browser test of the spreadsheet preview selects a cell with the keyboard instead of a mouse click before resizing, because a click could be re-applied against a changed layout and select the wrong cell.
firstReason: Upstream test maintenance: a repair of one browser test of a third-party spreadsheet widget.
